sheet.subtitle: Geothermal potential of Vojvodina: 3D model of hydrothermal wells

notes: **Position.** The annex lists settlements, not coordinates, so each well stands at the centre of its settlement. Wells of one settlement are spread on a ring about 2 km wide so that they can be told apart.

**Measured.** Each coloured bar is the temperature of the water at the tested interval. Where the annex gives no interval the marker is hollow and sits at the total depth; the temperature there is that of the water, which can have come from higher up, so the gradient at those wells is a lower bound.

**Atlas.** The layers, walls and contours are not measured at the wells. They come from the temperature maps at 500, 1,000 and 2,000 m of the [Geothermal Atlas of Vojvodina](https://www.psegs.vojvodina.gov.rs/wp-content/uploads/2013/03/Geothermal_atlas_of_AP_Vojvodina.pdf) (2010), digitised from the colour classes of the maps (steps of 0.5, 1 and 2 °C). Between the maps temperature rises in straight lines from 11 °C at the surface, which is assumed. Below 2 km, deeper than any map, it continues at the slope between 1 and 2 km. The bars on the wells (annex) and the colours (atlas) are different sources and do not always agree: the atlas is warmer than the annex water at 44 of 53 tests, by 9 °C on average.

**Shape and relief.** The outline is the boundary of AP Vojvodina from OpenStreetMap. The height of the ground is from Terrain Tiles on AWS (SRTM and other sources), on a 1 km grid, drawn above the median level of the province, 79 m, with the exaggeration set in the scale panel. The temperature layers are drawn as depth below that level and do not follow the ground; the difference matters only on Fruška Gora and the Vršac Mountains. The annex gives no elevations of the wells, so the wellheads sit on the ground model.

**Source.** Wells and tests are from [Prilog 1](https://www.psegs.vojvodina.gov.rs/wp-content/uploads/2013/03/Mogucnosti_koriscenja_energetskog_potencijala_geotermalnih_voda_u_AP_Vojvodini_-_prilog_1-_2005.pdf) of *Mogućnosti korišćenja energetskog potencijala geotermalnih voda u AP Vojvodini* (2005), records of NIS Naftagas supplied by the Provincial Secretariat for Energy and Mineral Resources, which published the study openly: 51 wells in three tables, Kž-2/H counted once.

background.heading: Engineering first, then code
paragraphs: I hold a degree in Mining Engineering from the University of Belgrade (graduated 2010). In 2026 the Bavarian Chamber of Engineers (Bayerische Ingenieurekammer-Bau) found my education equivalent to German requirements and granted me the professional title Ingenieur.

I started in 2011 as a mining engineer on mineral exploration projects, including underground work, then moved into drilling in 2012, planning and supervising exploration wells. Since 2013 I have worked in coiled tubing and nitrogen operations, from field engineer to operations manager, on more than 1,000 jobs. That work taught me how real operations behave: pressures, limits, and what breaks when a number is wrong. I bring that habit of checking the numbers into every website and tool I build.
For technical companies this means less explaining. You do not have to teach me what a job looks like on site before I can build the page for it.

nitrogenZ.title: Compressibility factor of nitrogen
nitrogenZ.intro: Z corrects the ideal gas law for nitrogen at high pressure: above 1 the gas takes more room than an ideal gas, so a vessel or well holds less nitrogen in standard volumes than with Z = 1. The diagram and the table give Z for nitrogen by absolute pressure and temperature; the nitrogen tools interpolate in the table.
nitrogenZ.chartLabel: Compressibility factor Z of nitrogen against absolute pressure, for five temperatures from −20 to 160 °C
nitrogenZ.marker: Orange point: the conditions of your calculation.
nitrogenZ.source: Computed from the density of nitrogen in the NIST Chemistry WebBook (equation of state of Span et al., 2000) as Z = P·M/(ρ·R·T). Pressures are absolute, gauge pressure plus 1.013 bar. Between the points the tools interpolate linearly; outside 1–500 bar and −20 to 160 °C they use the edge value.
nitrogenZ.hint: Z from the table at these conditions
nitrogenZ.outside: Outside the table: the value at the edge is shown.

meta.title: CT Strength Limits
meta.description: Check coiled tubing against burst, collapse and tension: stresses, von Mises equivalent stress and API collapse and burst limits, in oilfield or metric units.

hero.title: CT Strength Limits
hero.description: Stresses, burst, collapse and tension limits of coiled tubing for the load you enter, with the von Mises check against the yield factor. Oilfield or metric units.

ovality.label: Ovality
ovality.hint: (ODmax − ODmin) / OD; about 0.005 for new tubing

yieldStress.label: Yield strength
yieldStress.hint: Minimum yield strength of the steel

yieldFactor.label: Yield factor
yieldFactor.hint: Design factor on the yield strength

axialForce.label: Axial force
axialForce.hint: Positive in tension, negative in compression

bendingRadius.label: Bend radius
bendingRadius.hint: Radius the tubing is bent over; 0 for straight tubing

safetyFactor.label: Collapse safety factor
safetyFactor.hint: Safety factor of the API 5C7 collapse correction for tension, at least 1

method.title: Method
method.intro: The tubing is checked as a thick-walled steel tube under internal and external pressure, axial force and an optional bend.
steps: Axial stress is the axial force over the steel area. A bend of radius R adds the bending stress E·OD/(2R) on the convex side and subtracts it on the concave side; the larger absolute value is used.

Hoop and radial stress at the inside wall come from the Lamé equations for a thick cylinder; the radial stress there equals minus the internal pressure. The von Mises stress combines the three: √(σa² + σh² + σr² − σa·σh − σa·σr − σh·σr). Torque is not included.

Burst: API 5C3 internal yield 0.875 · 2Y·t/D; capped-end yield (4Y/√3)·(t/D)·(1 − t/D), where the von Mises stress at the inside wall reaches Y; true burst (2Y/√3)·ln(OD/ID), where the whole wall yields.

Collapse: Timoshenko, Pc = [Py·R + Pe·(1 + 3·ov·D/2t) − √((Py·R + Pe·(1 + 3·ov·D/2t))² − 4·Py·Pe·R)] / 2, with Py = 2Y·t/D, Pe = 2E/(1 − ν²)·(t/D)³ and R the reduction for axial stress; round tubing has ov = 0. API 5C3 uses the yield, plastic, transition or elastic range of D/t, with the yield strength reduced for axial stress. API RP 5C7 gives the collapse of oval tubing from the round collapse and the ovality, and in tension reduces it by Kcf = ((1/SF)^(4/3) − (L/Ly)^(4/3))^0.75.
Tension limits: Ly = yield factor · Y · steel area, and the largest axial force that keeps the von Mises stress at the yield factor with the hoop and radial stress of the entered pressures.
assumptions: A seamless steel tube with uniform wall and the nominal dimensions entered, without corrosion, wear or fatigue.
Pressures are uniform along the tubing; the stresses are those at the inside wall, the worst case.
Torque and shear stresses are not included.
The API collapse equations are valid for the D/t range of the standards; check results outside it.
method.reference: Based on the API 5C3 and API RP 5C7 equations, Timoshenko collapse, the Lamé equations and the von Mises criterion. The calculation reproduces a reference worksheet for its example case. Check the standards before you rely on a result; fatigue life is not covered.

meta.title: Nitrogen Displacement
meta.description: Calculate how much nitrogen is needed to displace the fluid in a well through coiled tubing: gas at standard conditions, as liquid nitrogen and by mass, in metric or oilfield units.

hero.title: Nitrogen Displacement
hero.description: How much nitrogen it takes to displace the fluid in a well through coiled tubing, including the tubing still on the reel. Metric or oilfield units.

ctLength.label: Coiled tubing on the reel
ctLength.hint: Total length, including what goes into the well

depth.label: Pumping depth
depth.hint: Depth the nitrogen is pumped from

fluidDensity.label: Fluid in the well
fluidDensity.hint: Density of the fluid being displaced

compressibility.label: Compressibility factor, Z
compressibility.hint: 1 for an ideal gas. Use the value from the table below.

nitrogenDensity.label: Mean nitrogen density in the well
nitrogenDensity.hint: Average density of the gas column; sets the pressure at the wellhead

results.title: Result
results.reel: Filling the tubing on the reel

method.title: Method
method.intro: The well fluid is displaced down to the pumping depth; the nitrogen that fills the column, and the tubing left on the reel, is totalled as gas, liquid and mass.
steps: Pressure at depth balances the hydrostatic column of the well fluid: P = ρ·g·h. The wellhead pressure is that minus the weight of the nitrogen column, from the mean nitrogen density. The column is taken at the mean of the two pressures and of the two temperatures.
Volume factor of nitrogen: B = 2.8416·P / (Z·(273 + T)) in sm³/m³, with P in kPa and T in °C. The constant stands for standard conditions of about 15 °C and 101.3 kPa.
Volume filled with gas: the production tubing bore minus the coiled tubing steel, times the depth. That is the annulus and the coiled tubing bore, each counted once.
Nitrogen for the well is that volume times the factor at mean conditions. Nitrogen for the tubing still on the reel is its bore volume times the factor at wellhead conditions.
Liquid nitrogen: 1 m³ of liquid gives 696.5 sm³ of gas and weighs 808 kg.
assumptions: The fluid is displaced completely down to the pumping depth, in a vertical well.
The compressibility factor is constant along the column; the temperature is the mean of the two ends.
The mean nitrogen density is an input, not derived from the pressure, so the wellhead pressure follows from it.
No fluid enters the well and no nitrogen is lost; nothing is allowed for the pumping losses or a reserve.
method.reference: Reproduces a reference worksheet, with one difference: the worksheet counts the coiled tubing bore twice in the volume filled with gas, which here is counted once, so the nitrogen for the well is lower than the worksheet’s. Check the gas properties against a nitrogen table before you rely on a result.

meta.title: Nitrogen for a Vessel
meta.description: Calculate the nitrogen needed to bring a vessel up to a pressure at a given temperature: gas at standard conditions, as liquid nitrogen and by mass, in metric or oilfield units.

hero.title: Nitrogen for a Vessel
hero.description: Enter the volume of a vessel, the pressure it is raised to and its temperature to get the nitrogen needed. Metric or oilfield units.

initialPressure.label: Starting pressure
initialPressure.hint: Gauge pressure; 0 for an empty vessel at atmospheric pressure

compressibility.label: Compressibility factor, Z
compressibility.hint: 1 for an ideal gas. Use the value from the table below.

results.title: Result
results.factor: Volume factor at the final pressure
results.gasInVessel: Gas in the vessel at the final pressure
results.gas: Gas to add, at standard conditions

method.title: Method
method.intro: The nitrogen is the gas that has to be added to take the vessel from its starting pressure to the final pressure at constant temperature.
steps: Volume factor of nitrogen: B = 2.8416·P / (Z·(273 + T)) in sm³/m³, with P in kPa (gauge) and T in °C. The constant stands for standard conditions of about 15 °C and 101.3 kPa.
Gas to add: the vessel volume times the difference of the factors at the final and at the starting pressure.
Liquid nitrogen: 1 m³ of liquid gives 696.5 sm³ of gas and weighs 808 kg.
assumptions: The pressures are gauge pressures and the vessel starts with no other gas than the air at atmospheric pressure, which is not counted.
The temperature stays constant while the vessel is filled; heating from compression is not allowed for.
The compressibility factor is a single value for the whole range of pressure.
No nitrogen is lost to purging or leaks.
method.reference: Uses the same volume factor and nitrogen properties as the Nitrogen Displacement tool, which reproduces a reference worksheet. Check the gas properties against a nitrogen table before you rely on a result.

meta.title: CT Pressure Loss
meta.description: Calculate the friction pressure loss of a Newtonian, Bingham plastic, power-law, Herschel–Bulkley or empirically measured fluid pumped through coiled tubing, split into straight and reel-wound sections, in oilfield or metric units.

hero.title: CT Pressure Loss
hero.description: Frictional pressure loss for fluids pumped through coiled tubing. Choose the rheology model, enter the fluid, the tubing and the flow rate, in oilfield or metric units.

n.label: Flow behaviour index, n
n.hint: Power-law exponent; 1 for a Newtonian fluid

k.label: Consistency index, K
k.hint: Power-law consistency, from the rheology of the fluid

reelDiameter.label: Reel diameter
reelDiameter.hint: Diameter of the coil the tubing is wound on

roughness.label: Wall roughness
roughness.hint: Absolute roughness of the inside wall; 0 for smooth tubing. Only affects turbulent flow

lengthOffReel.label: Tubing off the reel
lengthOffReel.hint: Straight length, not wound on the reel

model.label: Rheology model
model.hint: How the flow curve of the fluid is described

pv.label: Plastic viscosity (PV)
pv.hint: For a Newtonian fluid, its viscosity

fluidTemperature.label: Fluid temperature
fluidTemperature.hint: Temperature at which PV and YP are taken from the table; empty uses the values above

method.title: Method
method.intro: The loss is calculated separately for the part of the string off the reel (straight) and the part on the reel (curved), and the two are added.
steps: Rheology: the model gives the wall shear stress τ at a wall shear rate γ. Newtonian: τ = μγ. Bingham plastic: τ = YP + PV·γ. Power law: τ = Kγⁿ. Herschel–Bulkley: τ = τ₀ + Kγⁿ. Empirical: the measured Fann points joined by straight lines on log–log axes. Fann speed N rpm gives γ = 1.7023 N 1/s and τ = 1.0678 θ lbf/100 ft².

Equivalent power law: at the flow in question the pseudo shear rate is Γ = 8V/D. The wall shear rate γw = Γ(3n′+1)/(4n′) is found by iterating with n′, the local slope of the flow curve, and the model's K and n′ are those that give the same wall stress and slope. A power-law fluid returns its own n and K.

Fann fit: Bingham plastic PV = θ600 − θ300 and YP = θ300 − PV; Herschel–Bulkley τ₀ = 2τ3 − τ6 and a log–log fit for n and K; power law a log–log fit; Newtonian a fit through the origin. The deviation is the root-mean-square relative error of the model against the readings.
Reynolds number (Metzner–Reed): Re = 31.042 ρ Q^(2−n) / (9.804^n K ID^(4−3n)) · (n/(1+3n))^n, with ρ in lb/gal, Q in gal/min, ID in inches and K in lbf·sⁿ/100 ft².
Straight tubing: laminar below Re = 3470 − 1370n and turbulent above 4270 − 1370n. Laminar f = 16/Re. Turbulent f = a/Re^b, with a = (log n + 3.93)/50 and b = (1.75 − log n)/7.

Coiled tubing: the laminar factor is multiplied by ψ·De^φ, where De = Re_g·(ID/D)^0.5 is the Dean number, ψ = 47.969 − 153.8n + 166.22n² − 60.132n³ and φ = 0.875n − 0.515. Turbulent: f = 1.069·a/Re^(0.8b)·(ID/D)^0.1. The laminar limit is (4n/(3n+1))^n · [2100 ψ (ID/D)^(0.5φ)]^(1/(1−φ)) and the turbulent limit is 800 above it.

Pressure loss: ΔP = f ρ Q² L / (154.63 ID⁵) in oilfield units. Between the two limits the loss is interpolated linearly in Re, from the laminar loss at the lower limit to the turbulent loss at the upper limit.
assumptions: Wall roughness enters only the turbulent friction factor, as the ratio of the Haaland factor with roughness to the one without, so a roughness of 0 gives the smooth-tube result. For n other than 1 this is an estimate.

For models with a yield stress the equivalent power law is evaluated at the flow rate entered. This is sound for laminar flow; turbulent and transitional values for such fluids are estimates, and the critical Reynolds numbers are those of a power-law fluid.
A single-phase power-law fluid without solids.
Smooth tubing and fully developed flow, with fluid properties constant along the string.
The curvature is that of the reel diameter you enter; tubing off the reel is straight.
The correlations cover a limited range of n and ID/D. Check results outside it.
method.reference: Based on published correlations for power-law fluids in coiled tubing (Zhou and Shah), with the Metzner–Reed Reynolds number and Dodge–Metzner turbulent factors. The calculation reproduces a reference worksheet for its example case. Check the original papers before you rely on a result.

fann.note: Dial readings θ of a Fann 35 viscometer at each speed. The standard R1-B1 rotor-bob combination and F1 torsion spring are assumed.
fann.fit: Fit the model to the readings
fann.direct: The empirical model uses the readings directly.
fann.failed: The readings do not support this model. Enter all 12 readings, or at least 600 and 300 rpm for Bingham plastic.

temp.note: For Newtonian and Bingham fluids PV and YP are interpolated between the rows at the fluid temperature. Leave the table empty to use the surface values.

wMd.hint: Measured depth of the tubing shoe

wMargin.label: Overbalance
wMargin.hint: Pressure the kill fluid adds over the formation pressure

wInject.label: Injection pressure above formation
wInject.hint: Pressure above the formation pressure needed to push fluid into it when bullheading

wFracture.label: Fracture pressure
wFracture.hint: At the formation depth; 0 leaves the check out

dLeakoff.label: Leak-off, as mud density
dLeakoff.hint: Mud density equivalent to the leak-off pressure at the shoe

dSpm.hint: Strokes per minute at the kill rate

results.title: Result
results.hydrostatic: Hydrostatic pressure of the kill fluid
results.circulationTime: Time to pump tubing and annulus
results.startPressure: Surface pressure at the start of bullheading
results.endPressure: Surface pressure at the end of bullheading

schedule.title: Drill pipe pressure schedule
schedule.note: While the kill mud goes down the string, hold the drill pipe pressure to this schedule, then hold the final circulating pressure until the kill mud is at surface.

methods.label: Method
methods.hint: Producing well kill, or a drilling well killed by one of the two circulation methods

method.title: Method
method.intro: The tool calculates the kill from the balance of hydrostatic pressures.
steps: Hydrostatic pressure: P = ρ·g·TVD, with g = 9.80665 m/s². The formation pressure is the shut-in pressure plus the hydrostatic pressure of the fluid in the well.

Producing well: the kill fluid density balances the formation pressure plus the overbalance, ρ = (P + overbalance) / (g·TVD). Volumes are π/4·ID²·L for the tubing and π/4·(casing ID² − tubing OD²)·L for the annulus.

Bullheading: the surface pressure is the injection pressure (formation pressure plus the pressure needed to inject) minus the hydrostatic pressure of the fluid in the tubing. It starts at the shut-in pressure plus the injection margin and falls as the kill fluid goes in. The bottomhole pressure is checked against the fracture pressure.

Drilling well: kill mud density = mud density + SIDPP / (g·TVD). ICP = SIDPP + circulating pressure at the kill rate; FCP = circulating pressure × kill mud / mud density. The drill pipe pressure falls linearly from ICP to FCP over the strokes to the bit.

Wait and weight circulates once with the kill mud. The driller's method circulates the influx out with the original mud first, holding ICP, and then circulates the kill mud. MAASP = (leak-off density − mud density)·g·shoe TVD.
assumptions: A vertical column of one fluid: no gas in the fluid, no friction while bullheading and no temperature or compressibility effect on the density.
Pressures are gauge. Check the kill against the casing, tubing and wellhead pressure ratings.
The kill sheet is for the method the page names; choke operation and the response to a gas influx need judgement on location.
method.reference: This tool is a planning aid, not a substitute for the operator's well control procedures and the well control certification of the crew. Check the result against the company's own kill sheet.
